documentation.content:
# Telco Customer Churn

This study explores customer churn in a telecommunications dataset and develops an educational machine-learning model for estimating churn risk.

The objective is not only to obtain a predictive model, but to document the complete analytical path from understanding the dataset to evaluating a final model on previously unseen data.

## Dataset overview

Each row represents a telecommunications customer account.

| Item                |                 Value |
| ------------------- | --------------------: |
| Customer accounts   |                 7,043 |
| Source columns      |                    21 |
| Predictive features |                    19 |
| Target              |               `Churn` |
| Positive class      |         `Churn = Yes` |
| Churn prevalence    |                26.54% |
| Problem type        | Binary classification |

The customer identifier (`customerID`) is excluded from model inputs, and the target (`Churn`) is never exposed as a predictive feature.

The dataset includes information about:

* customer and household characteristics;
* relationship duration;
* phone and internet services;
* security, support, and streaming services;
* contract terms;
* billing preferences;
* payment methods;
* monthly and accumulated charges.

## Analytical question

The study investigates two related questions:

1. **Which characteristics are associated with customer churn in this dataset?**
2. **How effectively can those characteristics be used to estimate churn risk for unseen customer records?**

Exploratory findings are interpreted as associations within this dataset snapshot. They do not establish causal relationships or prove that changing an individual characteristic would change a customer's behavior.

## Data quality and preparation

The source contains 7,043 unique customer accounts with no duplicated customer identifiers.

A specific quality issue was identified in `TotalCharges`:

* 11 records contained blank values;
* all occurred for customers with `tenure == 0`;
* the blanks were deterministically materialized as `0.0`;
* no customer rows were removed;
* no generic statistical imputation was introduced.

The prepared data was reproducibly divided using stratification and random seed `42`:

| Partition  |  Rows | Purpose                                     |
| ---------- | ----: | ------------------------------------------- |
| Train      | 4,930 | Model development and cross-validation      |
| Validation | 1,056 | Candidate comparison and threshold analysis |
| Test       | 1,057 | Final evaluation only                       |

The test partition remained sealed during feature analysis, model selection, hyperparameter selection, and threshold selection.

## Churn distribution

Churn is the minority class in the dataset.

Of the 7,043 customer accounts, 1,869 have `Churn = Yes`, corresponding to a prevalence of approximately **26.54%**.

![Distribution of the Churn target classes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-telco-customer-churn/main/docs/images/churn_target_class_distribution.png)

Because of this imbalance, model selection does not rely on accuracy alone. Average Precision is used as the primary selection metric, supported by ROC-AUC, Brier Score and other classification metrics.

## Key exploratory findings

### Contract type has a strong association with churn

Churn rates vary substantially across contract categories:

| Contract       | Churn rate |
| -------------- | ---------: |
| Month-to-month |     42.71% |
| One year       |     11.27% |
| Two year       |      2.83% |

![Churn rate by contract category](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-telco-customer-churn/main/docs/images/contract_churn_rate_by_category.png)

Month-to-month customers show considerably higher observed churn than customers with one-year or two-year contracts.

This is an association in the observed data and must not be interpreted as proof that changing a customer's contract would independently prevent churn.

### Churn is concentrated earlier in the customer relationship

Customers who churn tend to have substantially shorter observed tenure.

Across tenure quantiles, churn decreases from approximately **58.4%** in the earliest-tenure group to approximately **3.5%** in the longest-tenure group.

![Churn rate by tenure quantile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-telco-customer-churn/main/docs/images/tenure_churn_rate_by_quantile.png)

The beginning of the customer relationship therefore emerges as an important analytical region.

Tenure itself should still be interpreted carefully: remaining a customer naturally increases tenure, so this relationship does not establish a causal retention effect.

### Service and billing characteristics add predictive signal

Contract type is not the only characteristic associated with churn.

Other notable categorical associations include:

* online security;
* technical support;
* internet service;
* payment method.

![Ranking of categorical feature associations with churn](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FabioAguiar/dataset-study-telco-customer-churn/main/docs/images/feature_to_target_categorical_association_ranking.png)

These relationships indicate that churn behavior in this dataset is distributed across customer relationship, service, contract, and billing dimensions rather than being explained by a single feature.

## Model selection

The study compares a prior-only baseline with four machine-learning model families:

| Model                    | Validation Average Precision | Validation ROC-AUC | Brier Score ↓ |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------: | -----------------: | ------------: |
| **HistGradientBoosting** |                   **0.6708** |         **0.8477** |    **0.1332** |
| Logistic Regression      |                       0.6688 |             0.8470 |        0.1339 |
| Random Forest            |                       0.6679 |             0.8475 |        0.1593 |
| Decision Tree            |                       0.6134 |             0.8161 |        0.1462 |
| Dummy prior              |                       0.2652 |             0.5000 |        0.1948 |

Average Precision was the primary model-selection metric because churn is the minority class.

`HistGradientBoostingClassifier` and Logistic Regression produced a **practical tie** in validation Average Precision.

HistGradientBoosting was selected using the predefined tie-break rule because it achieved the lower Brier Score.

The selected model is therefore not simply the model associated with the numerically largest metric shown on the page; selection follows the evaluation policy defined by the study.

## Final model evaluation

After model selection, the chosen pipeline was trained using the combined train and validation data and evaluated once on the previously sealed test partition.

| Metric            | Validation | Final test |
| ----------------- | ---------: | ---------: |
| Average Precision |     0.6708 | **0.6413** |
| ROC-AUC           |     0.8477 | **0.8402** |
| Brier Score ↓     |     0.1332 | **0.1394** |
| Log Loss ↓        |     0.4135 | **0.4207** |

The model maintained useful ranking performance on unseen test data.

The modest difference between validation and final-test results does not indicate a performance collapse under this particular random-snapshot evaluation.

These results do not establish temporal or production generalization.

## Understanding the highlighted metrics

### PR-AUC / Average Precision — 0.6413

Average Precision summarizes how effectively the model retrieves churn cases while maintaining precision across classification thresholds.

Because churn represents approximately 26.5% of the dataset, this metric is especially informative for evaluating the minority positive class.

**Higher values are better.**

### ROC-AUC — 0.8402

ROC-AUC measures the model's ability to rank churn customers above non-churn customers across thresholds.

A value of `0.8402` indicates useful discrimination in the final holdout evaluation.

**Higher values are better.**

The fact that ROC-AUC is numerically higher than Average Precision does not mean it was automatically the more appropriate metric for model selection. The metrics measure different properties and should not be compared by their raw numerical magnitude.

## Educational classification threshold

The study also evaluates an educational threshold of:

`0.2578`

This threshold was selected using validation data to achieve a recall target of at least 80%.

On the final test set:

| Metric            | Threshold 0.50 | Educational threshold 0.2578 |
| ----------------- | -------------: | ---------------------------: |
| Precision         |         62.50% |                       51.25% |
| Recall            |         49.82% |                       80.43% |
| F1                |         55.45% |                       62.60% |
| F2                |         51.93% |                       72.20% |
| Balanced accuracy |         69.50% |                       76.36% |

Reducing the threshold identifies more customers who churned, but it also generates substantially more false positives.

At the educational threshold, 86 additional churn cases are identified compared with the `0.50` threshold, while 131 additional false positives are produced.

This illustrates an important property of classification systems: **the prediction threshold represents a trade-off rather than a universally optimal value.**

Selecting an operational threshold would require information that this dataset does not provide, including intervention costs, customer value, campaign capacity, and the relative cost of false-positive and false-negative decisions.

## Inference experience

The Atlas inference form uses the trained model to demonstrate how customer characteristics are transformed into a churn-risk estimate.

The model receives 19 customer characteristics covering profile, relationship, connectivity, online services, contract, billing, and charges.

The inference result should be interpreted as an **educational demonstration of the trained model**, not as an operational recommendation about an actual customer.

The model pipeline includes both preprocessing and classification, allowing the same transformation learned during training to be applied consistently during inference.

## What this study demonstrates

The project establishes an end-to-end educational workflow for:

* dataset understanding and exploratory analysis;
* explicit data-quality decisions;
* deterministic data preparation;
* leakage prevention;
* isolated train, validation, and test partitions;
* model comparison;
* metric-aware model selection;
* final holdout evaluation;
* model serialization;
* contract-driven inference.

The study therefore documents not only the final model, but also the reasoning and evidence used to reach it.

## Limitations

Several important questions remain outside the scope of the current study:

* evaluation is based on a stratified random snapshot rather than a temporal holdout;
* exploratory associations do not establish causal effects;
* production-time feature availability has not been established;
* the educational threshold is not an operational business policy;
* false-positive and false-negative business costs are unknown;
* no retention-intervention or uplift study has been performed;
* deployment fairness and subgroup stability have not been established;
* no drift-monitoring or scheduled-retraining policy exists.

These limitations prevent the current analysis from supporting automated customer-retention decisions.

## Responsible interpretation

The evidence supports the following conclusion:

> In this educational dataset snapshot, churn is strongly associated with shorter customer tenure, month-to-month contracts, and selected service and billing characteristics. HistGradientBoosting was selected in a practical validation tie with Logistic Regression and achieved a final-test Average Precision of 0.6413 and ROC-AUC of 0.8402. A lower educational threshold substantially increases churn recall while also increasing false positives, so the current study does not justify an operational threshold or automated retention action.

The Atlas inference experience should therefore be understood as an interactive representation of the predictive study and its contracts, rather than as a production customer-decision system.
